title: GEO as a threat surface
excerpt: New research shows that deep research agents can be "poisoned" to shift what gets cited.
html:
Seven months ago, 76% of the pages Google cited in AI Overviews came from the organic top 10.

That figure is now 38%.

We've been talking about the gap between rankings and AI visibility for a while. But this rate of collapse — in under a year — is something I don't think most SEO teams have fully reckoned with yet. Ranking well and being cited in AI answers are becoming genuinely separate disciplines, requiring different signals, different content structures and different measurement entirely.

It gets more interesting. Only 17% of AIO citations currently come from the organic top 10 at all. Which means the other 83% of what AI Overviews cites is coming from somewhere your rank tracker isn't watching.

Then this week a new arXiv paper added a dimension I haven't seen discussed much in the industry. Researchers demonstrated that deep-research AI agents can be "poisoned" via manipulated user-generated content — Reddit threads, forum posts, reviews — to shift what gets cited and recommended. The authors frame it explicitly as the generative-AI equivalent of black-hat SEO.

So GEO is no longer just an opportunity. It's also a threat surface.

Brands that are invisible in AI answers right now aren't just missing traffic. They're leaving a vacuum that others — including bad actors — are already working out how to fill.

The question I keep coming back to: how many teams are building a GEO strategy at all, let alone a defensive one?

title: E-E-A-T: The credibility layer
excerpt: Most discussions of AI search optimisation focus on what machines can read: structured data, heading hierarchies, metadata. But there's a layer underneath all of that — one that determines whether an AI system considers your content credible enough to cite in the first place. That layer has a name: E-E-A-T.
html:
Why AI search needs humans to decide what's worth quoting

Most discussions of AI search optimisation focus on what machines can read: structured data, heading hierarchies, metadata. But there's a layer underneath all of that — one that determines whether an AI system considers your content credible enough to cite in the first place. That layer has a name: E-E-A-T.

What E-E-A-T actually is

E-E-A-T stands for Experience, Expertise, Authoritativeness, and Trustworthiness. It originates in Google's Search Quality Rater Guidelines — a document used to train human evaluators who assess whether pages genuinely serve users well. The framework gained its first "E" (Experience) in December 2022, reflecting a growing emphasis on first-hand knowledge over secondhand aggregation.

The four signals work as a hierarchy, but Trust sits at the top. A page can appear experienced and authoritative and still fail if the underlying content is inaccurate, anonymous, or lacking clear provenance.

The human-in-the-loop you didn't know about

Here's where it gets interesting from an AI perspective. E-E-A-T is not an algorithm. It is a framework applied by human quality raters — contractors who manually review pages and score them against Google's guidelines. Their assessments don't directly affect individual rankings, but they feed into how Google trains and calibrates its ranking systems over time.

This makes E-E-A-T one of the clearest examples of human-in-the-loop design in production AI. The outputs of these evaluations shape what the model learns to reward — meaning the entire edifice of AI-generated search results rests, in part, on human judgement about what trustworthy content looks like. That's a meaningful architectural choice, and it has practical implications for how you build content.

What it means for AIO

The signals that quality raters look for map almost directly onto what AI Overviews and answer engines use when deciding what to cite. Clear authorship. Named expertise. Transparency about methodology, sources, and perspective. Content that demonstrates the author has actually done the thing rather than synthesised it from elsewhere.

This last point — Experience — is where the most recent updates have added pressure. Generic, abstract content that reads as competent but impersonal is increasingly scrutinised. Content with clear first-hand grounding: dated accounts, named locations, specific outcomes, attributed perspectives — this is what both human raters and the systems they train are looking for.

The practical implication: treat your About page, author bio, and any methodology you describe not as supporting material, but as core E-E-A-T infrastructure. These are the signals that tell both humans and machines whether your content is worth quoting — or merely worth reading.

One important nuance: E-E-A-T is an evaluative framework, not a direct ranking signal. You cannot "add E-E-A-T" to a page the way you add schema markup. What you can do is ensure the signals it looks for are present, visible, and honest.

title: From SEO to GEO: Why JSON-LD Is the Hidden Layer Behind AI Visibility
excerpt: Learn about the importance of JSON-LD schema for making websites discoverable by generative AI platforms.
html:
JSON-LD schema has quietly become one of the most important tools for online discoverability — not just for search engines, but for AI systems and large language models (LLMs) as well.

In simple terms, JSON-LD is structured data that helps machines understand what your website content actually means. Rather than forcing AI systems to “guess” whether a page is about a product, article, organization, or service, schema provides explicit context. That clarity is increasingly valuable in the era of AI-generated answers and conversational search.

Modern LLMs don’t just scan keywords. They look for signals of authority, relevance, and structure. Well-implemented schema helps these systems identify:

  • Who your business is
  • What your pages are about
  • Which content is authoritative
  • How different pieces of information connect together

The result? Improved discoverability, more accurate AI summaries, and a greater chance of being surfaced in generative search experiences.

For businesses investing heavily in content, failing to implement structured data is like publishing a book without chapter titles. Your information may still exist online, but AI systems are far less likely to interpret it correctly or prioritize it confidently.

This is especially important when combined with emerging GEO practices such as llms.txt files. While llms.txt helps guide AI systems toward your preferred content and positioning, JSON-LD schema provides the semantic structure that helps those systems understand your site at a deeper level. Together, they create a stronger foundation for AI visibility.

The technical setup itself is relatively straightforward. The real value lies in strategy: choosing the right schema types, aligning them with your authority goals, and ensuring AI systems consistently interpret your brand the way you intend.

That’s where a professional GEO audit becomes valuable. Many websites already have schema installed — but very few are truly optimized for AI-driven discovery.

title: The importance of having an llms.txt file
excerpt: Why you need an llms.txt file if you're serious about GEO discoverability.
html:
An llms.txt file might sound niche today, but it’s quickly becoming a critical part of modern SEO and GEO strategy. As AI-driven search tools like OpenAI ChatGPT, Google Gemini, and other large language models increasingly shape how users discover information, websites need clearer ways to communicate with these systems.

Think of llms.txt as a guidebook for AI. It helps language models understand which parts of your site matter most, which content is authoritative, and how your information should be interpreted. While traditional SEO focused on search engine crawlers, GEO (Generative Engine Optimization) is about influencing how AI systems summarize, cite, and recommend your brand.

A strong llms.txt file typically includes:

Your preferred site description and expertise areas Key URLs and priority content sections Citation preferences and canonical resources Guidance on structured content or documentation Instructions that reduce AI confusion or hallucination risks

The goal isn’t just visibility — it’s accuracy. Without clear signals, AI tools may misunderstand your content, overlook valuable pages, or fail to associate your brand with the topics you want to own.

Implementation itself is relatively simple, but strategy is where most businesses fall short. The real challenge is deciding what AI systems should prioritize and how that aligns with your broader SEO, content, and authority-building efforts.

That’s why forward-thinking brands are beginning to audit their sites specifically for AI discoverability, not just search rankings. An llms.txt file is no longer a “future-proofing” exercise — it’s becoming part of building a resilient online presence in the AI era.

If you’re unsure whether your website is truly optimized for AI-driven discovery, a professional GEO audit can reveal gaps traditional SEO tools often miss.

title: What Is Generative Engine Optimisation (GEO)?
excerpt: GEO is the practice of optimising your content to be cited by AI-powered search engines and large language models. Here's what you need to know.
html:
What is GEO — and why does your website need it?

Search has changed. When someone types a question into Google, ChatGPT, or Perplexity today, they often receive a direct answer — synthesised, confident, and sourced from a handful of trusted pages. Your website may rank on page one and still be invisible in that response. That's the problem GEO is designed to solve.

Generative Engine Optimisation (GEO) is the practice of structuring your website so that AI-powered search engines can understand, trust, and cite your content. Where traditional SEO focuses on getting pages to rank, GEO focuses on getting content to be used — pulled into AI Overviews, featured in chatbot responses, and quoted by the large language models that an increasing proportion of your potential audience now relies on for answers.

Why it matters right now

AI search adoption is accelerating rapidly. Tools like Google's AI Overviews, Perplexity, and ChatGPT Search are reshaping how people find information — and they are highly selective about their sources. Pages that lack clear structure, authoritative signals, and machine-readable context are simply passed over, regardless of their traditional search ranking.

GEO isn't a replacement for SEO. It's the next layer. And the websites that get ahead of this shift now will hold a significant advantage as AI-mediated discovery becomes the norm.

What a GEO audit covers

A proper GEO audit examines how well your site communicates with AI systems — from your structured data and metadata to your content architecture, entity signals, and crawlability. It identifies exactly where you're losing visibility and what to do about it.
